questions.q: What does VACUUM do to a Redshift table?
options: Changes the table's DISTKEY automatically
Deletes the table's statistics
Copies the table's data into S3
Reclaims space from deleted/updated rows and re-sorts rows back into SORTKEY order
questions.explain: VACUUM reclaims space left by updates/deletes and restores physical row order to match the SORTKEY, since new writes land at the end of the table.

questions.q: Why does ANALYZE matter for query performance?
options: It compresses the table's stored data
It updates the table statistics the query planner uses to choose join algorithms and scan strategy
It automatically rewrites slow SQL queries
It has no effect on the query planner
questions.explain: Stale statistics after a large load or delete can lead the planner to pick a bad execution plan, even with well-chosen keys.

questions.q: In an EXPLAIN plan, a large data shuffle between nodes during a join usually points to what problem?
options: The table is missing a SORTKEY entirely
The DISTKEY doesn't match the join column
VACUUM has never been run
The cluster is using Redshift Serverless
questions.explain: When join keys don't align with the DISTKEY, matching rows aren't colocated on the same slice, forcing data to shuffle across the network.

questions.q: Why is an accidental cross join so expensive?
options: It only affects Redshift Serverless, not provisioned clusters
It disables columnar storage for that query
The result size multiplies row counts together instead of just combining matching rows
It always fails with an error before returning any rows
questions.explain: A cross join pairs every row of one table with every row of another, so two 100,000-row tables produce ten billion result rows.

options: Runs the query and returns the results faster than normal
Automatically fixes a bad DISTKEY
Runs VACUUM and ANALYZE together
Shows the query's execution plan without running the query
questions.explain: EXPLAIN reveals the plan the optimizer chose — scan types, join strategy, data movement — turning a vague slowdown into a visible, specific cause.
